implementation_notes: std::time::Instant is monotonic but has no timer, so the async runtime supplies both halves: tokio::time::timeout_at(Instant, future) fails with Elapsed when a future outlives an absolute instant - the right shape for propagation, since the instant is computed once and passed down - and tokio_util::sync::CancellationToken is the cancellation carrier, with child_token() producing descendants that are cancelled when the parent is. A hop wraps each downstream future in timeout_at(deadline) and selects on token.cancelled() for the caller-driven path; the docs note that cancelling a timeout is done by dropping the future, with no additional cleanup. The classic thread-plus-channel shutdown dance is replaced by structured cancellation around the request.
pitfalls: timeout_at requires a Tokio timer context: calling it outside a runtime (or with time disabled on the Builder) panics, so enable_time/enable_all and keep the call inside the runtime.

Dropping the future is the cancellation mechanism, but futures spawned with tokio::spawn keep running unless they hold their own token - keep the work structured (JoinSet/TaskTracker) or pass the token explicitly.
CancellationToken is clonable and child_token() propagates downward: a clone stored in a task that is never cancelled leaks work, so cancel the root at the request scope.
Blocking calls (std::fs, blocking database drivers) ignore the async deadline and hold the worker; move them to spawn_blocking with an explicit remaining-time timeout.
